trans-unit.source: Peripateticware began as a white paper written inside McGraw-Hill Education. It argued that GPS-enabled mobile devices would transform learning — that students walking through real places, guided by structured inquiry, could learn in a way textbooks never allowed.
trans-unit.target: Peripateticware بEGIN كتاب أفضل صورة خاصة، نشره في مجلة McGraw-Hill Education. وهو يقول عن أن الحدث الذي يسمح بتغيير التعلم، أن يكون طالبات تخرج إلى المكانات الحقيقية في حالة التدقيق المنهجي يمكنهم تعلم بأشكال كتب التعليم التي لم تستطيع أن تتعلم بها أولاً.

trans-unit.source: The paper named one problem it couldn't solve: assessment. How do you evaluate learning that happens in a creek bed, or at a cathedral arch, or in a city park? In 2026, AI finally gave us the answer.

trans-unit.target: , كيفية تقييم التعلم الذي ينطلق من محور ضيف، أو من خواص مزدوجة، أو من محطة شارك،؟ في 2026، ستوضع إي آي أي البريدة لنا الجواب.

trans-unit.source: The paper was written at a moment when 3G hadn't fully rolled out, the iPhone was months away from launch, and "app" wasn't yet a common word. Its predictions — that cell phones would become 1-for-1 classroom devices, that mobile networks would reach remote regions, that GPS would become cheap enough to put in every student's pocket — all came true. The products the paper called for did not.

trans-unit.source: If students follow their curiosity through real places, learning about arches, barrels, and celestial navigation because they're standing near a cathedral or a harbour, how do you assess what they've learned in a way that satisfies curriculum requirements? How do you produce the spreadsheet of numbers the principal wants while also honouring the complexity of what the student actually understood?

trans-unit.source: The document left that question open. The school system didn't solve it either. For nearly two decades, "outdoor learning" remained either a vague aspiration or a logistical nightmare — teachers with clipboards, activities that produced no artifact, experiences that disappeared the moment students came back inside.

trans-unit.source: The assessment problem turned out to have two parts. The first was capturing evidence — what did the student actually observe, and can you prove it? The second was evaluating it — did their thinking deepen, or did they just describe what they saw?
trans-unit.target: تدحّث مسؤولة القيام بتقييم إجرى مشكلة مرتبطة بها، أو يمكن أن تتعرف عليها.

trans-unit.source: The first part was solved by smartphones. Photo, audio, GPS coordinates, timestamps — a student at a creek bank can capture more evidence in ten minutes than a field trip clipboard could hold in a day. What remained was the second part: structured inquiry that didn't just document experience but deepened it.

That's where Peri comes in. Peri is Peripateticware's AI guide — named, like the software, after the Aristotelian method. Peri doesn't answer questions. It asks them. It follows the five-phase inquiry sequence — Engage, Observe, Analyse, Explain, Apply — that Aristotle used in the Lyceum and that cognitive science has since validated as a path to genuine understanding, not just retention. Peri takes a student's observation and asks the next right question. When the student gets it right, Peri tests the implication. When the student is vague, Peri asks for evidence.
trans-unit.target: هناك هو برسيبيتي. برسيبيتي المعلّق عن تدريس الخارج. برسيبيتي المعلّق عن تدريس الخارج هو Peri. Peri هو مُصدر AI في Peripateticware، يدعى كما تحتوي برنامج على أسمه. Peri لا يجوز السؤال. يسأل. يتم تطوير مشرقة في خطوات التحقيق خمسة: تناقض، تعلم، تفكيك، تفسير، وتطبيق. Peri يتأهل بطلبة تجربة شخصية ويسأل المزيد. إذا كان معلم يفاء، يتحقق Peri من تفاهم الإثناء. إذا كان معلم يكون ضدًّا بالواقع، يسأل Peri عن الأثر.

trans-unit.source: The result is an artifact: a field journal entry with captures, extended analysis, and a record of the inquiry itself. Teachers can see not just what a student concluded but how they got there. Rubrics aligned to Bloom's taxonomy and standards frameworks — CCSS, NGSS, TEKS, or your own — make the assessment legible to any curriculum coordinator. The spreadsheet and the real learning finally occupy the same document.

The 2007 paper described a "choose your own adventure" model of learning — one where students follow tangents, pursue what interests them, and encounter core curriculum concepts through the side doors of genuine curiosity rather than the front door of instruction. The paper acknowledged this was "somewhat chaotic" and that it would require new kinds of instructional design, new assessment tools, and teachers willing to trade some control for authentic engagement.
